title: One flash of anger
hook: a pan of oil left a moment too long, and the smell of smoke; Shantideva opens his chapter on patience with fire
tomorrow: if it can be fixed, why worry? and if it can't?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body as a boat: not worshipped, not wrecked, patched and sailing for good. A boat, not an idol. Today a new chapter opens, the one on patience, and it opens with fire.
screen: `A BOAT, NOT AN IDOL.` → `CHAPTER SIX: PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Anyone who's cooked knows the smell. Oil in a pan, left one moment too long while you answered a text. First a shimmer, then a thin gray thread of smoke, and then, faster than seems fair, a flame. A kitchen that took years to make into a home can be blackened in a minute. So how much good can a single flash of anger burn? Shantideva answers on the very first line of chapter six, and his answer is fire.
screen: `OIL, ONE MOMENT TOO LONG.` → `A THREAD OF SMOKE.` → `HOW MUCH CAN ONE FLASH BURN?`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, close to his words. All the good you've gathered over ages and ages, generosity, honoring the Buddhas, every kind act, one moment of anger can destroy. Then the next verse: there is no wrong like hatred, and no discipline like patience. It's meant to land like heat on the skin. Not a slow fade. A flash. And he keeps going, almost like a doctor listing symptoms. Someone gripped by anger finds no peace of mind, no joy, no ease. Sleep won't come. Even people who depend on their kindness may turn against them. Notice where the fire burns first. Not mostly the other person. It burns the one holding it. So the work of patience begins in a very physical place: the warmth in the face, the tight jaw, the heat rising in the chest. That's the smoke before the flame. You don't have to win an argument with the anger. You just need to notice the shimmer in the pan, early, while turning down the heat is still easy. One flash burns much. One noticed flash burns much less.
screen: `ONE MOMENT CAN DESTROY IT.` · `NO DISCIPLINE LIKE PATIENCE.` · `NO PEACE, NO SLEEP.` · `NOTICE THE SHIMMER IN THE PAN.` · then, large: `ONE FLASH BURNS MUCH.`

segments.voice: Rub your palms together fast, about ten times, until they're warm. Then hold them still, an inch apart, and feel the heat. Stay with that warmth as it slowly fades, the way a flash of anger fades when nothing is added to it.
One flash of anger: chapter six's opening warning. A moment of hatred can burn up a great deal of good, beginning with your own peace.
Carry this one: one flash burns much, so watch for the shimmer in the pan. Patience has begun.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists study Shantideva's sixth chapter as a core teaching on patience (kshanti), and Tibetan teachers often open lessons on anger with its first verses.

Shantideva lists what it does to the one holding it: no peace, no joy, no sleep.

it's the second verse of the chapter: no wrong like hatred, no discipline like patience.

fork.setup: your dad cuts you off mid-sentence at dinner, again, and you feel your face go hot. you've got about a second. what's the chapter-six move?
options: let it out now; holding anger in is what really hurts you.
notice the heat, the shimmer in the pan, and turn it down before it flames.
pretend nothing happened and change the subject cheerfully.
fork.reveal: Shantideva's patience starts with noticing the heat early. it isn't pretending, and it isn't letting the flash burn.

original.note: Sanskrit: anger, wrath. Chapter six names it among the strongest forces patience meets.

chat.meaning: Shantideva: one moment of anger can burn up much good, beginning with your own peace. Noticing the heat early is where patience starts.

Shantideva.meaning: Buddhist poet-monk who wrote this guide to the bodhisattva's way

Buddhas.meaning: fully awakened beings; honoring them is a kind of good work

patience.meaning: kshanti: bearing hurt and hardship without hatred

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 6.1-6.5 (a single moment of hatred destroys good deeds gathered over eons; there is no evil like hatred and no austerity like patience; the angry find no peace, joy or sleep; even dependents may turn on them)

notes: 6.1 says good gathered over 'a thousand eons' (sahasra-kalpa) in many translations; the lesson says 'ages and ages' to avoid stating a number. Confirm.
6.2 rendered 'no wrong like hatred, no discipline like patience' (austerity/tapas often translated 'discipline'). Confirm the wording.
6.3-6.5 paraphrased (no peace, joy or sleep; dependents may turn on the angry). Confirm.
